learning_objective: 🎯 Understand the powerful internal and external forces that constantly mold, break, and rebuild the beautiful landscapes of our planet!

main_concepts.simple_explanation: These are forces originating deep inside the Earth. They cause sudden movements like earthquakes and volcanic eruptions, or slow movements that build massive mountains.

The Earth's crust (Lithosphere) is broken into giant puzzle pieces called tectonic plates. They float and move over the molten mantle. When they crash, pull apart, or slide past each other, they shape the Earth's surface.
These are forces acting on the surface of the Earth, mainly driven by solar energy. Wind, water, and ice constantly wear down the land.
Weathering is the breaking down of rocks at their exact location (by temperature or plants). Erosion is the carrying away of these broken rock particles by rivers, winds, or glaciers.
The interaction of internal and external forces creates Mountains (high elevation), Plateaus (flat-topped tablelands), and Plains (low, flat areas great for farming).

fun_activity.title: 🧩 The Biscuit Tectonics
fun_activity.instructions: Take two biscuits and some thick jam. Place the biscuits on the jam. Push them together so one slides under the other, or pull them apart. You just recreated how tectonic plates move and create mountains!

exam_tips: 📌 Clearly differentiate between Endogenic (Inside) and Exogenic (Outside) forces.
📌 'Weathering is breaking, Erosion is taking.' Memorize this phrase to never confuse the two terms!
📌 Mountains are generally formed by Endogenic forces (folding/faulting), while plains are often formed by Exogenic forces (river deposits).
quick_recap: ⭐ The Earth's surface is never completely still; it is constantly changing.
⭐ The Himalayas were formed by the collision of the Indian and Eurasian tectonic plates.
⭐ Rivers are the most powerful agents of erosion, creating V-shaped valleys and deltas.
